insider_note: This is a standard Tan⁻¹ form; the answer stays in terms of a because the limits themselves depend on a.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Apply the standard formula
steps.margin_note: First mark. ∫dx/(x²+a²) = (1/a)Tan⁻¹(x/a) + c — one of the standard integration formulas.
steps.memory_tip: 1/(x² + a²) gives (1/a)Tan⁻¹(x/a); 1/√(a² − x²), a difference under a square root, gives Sin⁻¹(x/a).
lines: The denominator is a sum of two squares:
steps.why: The integral of 1/(x²+a²) is a standard form with antiderivative (1/a)Tan⁻¹(x/a), which is worth memorising directly rather than re-deriving each time.
common_mistakes: Writing the antiderivative as Tan⁻¹(x/a) without the leading 1/a.

steps.label: Apply the limits
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Tan⁻¹1 = π/4 — the same standard value used throughout this chapter.
steps.memory_tip: x/a at the upper limit x=a is always 1, giving Tan⁻¹1=π/4 regardless of the value of a.
steps.why: At the upper limit x=a, x/a=1 so Tan⁻¹(1)=π/4; at the lower limit x=0, Tan⁻¹(0)=0, so the bracket simplifies to π/4 and the outer 1/a gives the final answer.
common_mistakes: Using Tan⁻¹(1) = π/2 instead of the correct value π/4.
Forgetting the outer factor 1/a in the final answer.
